entry: [[Chemical element]] with atomic number 91 and symbol Pa. It is a dense, radioactive, silvery-gray [[Actinide|actinide]] metal that readily reacts with [[Oxygen|oxygen]], water vapor and inorganic acids. Its concentration in the Earth's crust is typically a few parts per trillion. It has no uses outside scientific research and is mostly extracted from spent nuclear fuel. The element was first identified in 1913 by Kazimierz Fajans and Oswald Helmuth Göhring, who named it "brevium" for the short half-life of the isotope studied. The more stable isotope 231Pa was discovered in 1917/18 by Lise Meitner and Otto Hahn; in 1949 the IUPAC confirmed them as discoverers and chose the name protactinium, meaning "(nuclear) precursor of actinium." Its most abundant natural isotope, 231Pa, has a half-life of 32,760 years. Ocean science uses its isotopes in radiometric dating of sediments up to 175,000 years old.

Family of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] predominantly distributed in the Southern Hemisphere. It comprises 83 [[Genus|genera]] with about 1,660 known [[Species|species]], and [[Australia]] and [[South Africa]] have the greatest concentrations of diversity. Well-known genera include *Protea*, *Banksia*, *Grevillea*, *Hakea* and [[Macadamia]]. The family is placed in the order Proteales, whose placement has varied, and is divided into five subfamilies. Robert Brown adapted the name Proteaceae from Proteae, coined in 1789 by Antoine Laurent de Jussieu. Several species, such as the [[New South Wales]] waratah and king protea, are popular cut flowers, and the nuts of *Macadamia integrifolia* are widely grown commercially, as are those of *Gevuina avellana* on a smaller scale.

[[Economic policy]] of restricting imports through tariffs, import quotas and other government regulations. Proponents argue that it shields domestic producers and workers from foreign competition and raises government revenue, while opponents argue that it reduces [[Trade|trade]] and raises the cost of imported goods for consumers. It has been advocated mainly by economic nationalist parties, and economically liberal parties generally support free trade. There is a consensus among economists that protectionism reduces [[Economic growth|economic growth]] and welfare. Douglas Irwin has implicated it as an important contributing factor in some economic crises, most notably the [[Great Depression]], although Paul Krugman argues that tariffs were a response to the Depression rather than its main cause. Free trade lowers costs for producers and consumers, though trade liberalization can cause short-run dislocation of workers in import-competing sectors.

Essential nutrient that forms part of body tissue and also serves as a fuel source. As fuel, it has the same energy density as [[Carbohydrate|carbohydrates]], 17 kJ (4 kcal) per gram. Its defining nutritional feature is its [[Amino acid|amino acid]] composition, and protein content in foods is usually measured by nitrogen content. Proteins are [[Polymer|polymer]] chains of amino acids linked by [[Peptide|peptide]] bonds. During digestion they are broken down in the [[Stomach|stomach]] by [[Hydrochloric acid|hydrochloric acid]] and protease enzymes. Nine essential amino acids cannot be synthesized by the body and must come from the diet, including lysine, leucine and histidine. After water, proteins make up more of an organism's mass than any other type of molecule, and they are structural components of every body tissue and organ. Plant protein foods supply over 60% of the per capita protein worldwide.

Geologic eon spanning 2500 to 538.8 million years ago, the longest eon of Earth's history. It is the third of four eons, within the [[Precambrian]] supereon. The eon runs from the appearance of free [[Oxygen|oxygen]] in the atmosphere to just before the [[Cambrian explosion|Cambrian Explosion]] of complex life. Its three eras are the Paleoproterozoic, Mesoproterozoic and Neoproterozoic. Key events include [[Eukaryote|eukaryote]] evolution through symbiogenesis and several global glaciations, including the hypothesized [[Snowball Earth]]. The [[Ediacaran]] period (635 to 538.8 million years ago) saw abundant soft-bodied multicellular organisms, the first obvious fossil evidence of life on Earth.

Public act of objection, disapproval or dissent against political advantage. Also called a demonstration or remonstrance, a protest can range from individual statements to mass political demonstrations. Protesters may seek to influence public opinion or government policy, or they may take direct action to enact desired changes themselves. When protests form part of a systematic, peaceful nonviolent campaign that uses pressure as well as persuasion, they may be described as civil resistance. Government policy sometimes restricts protest, such as through permit requirements, and states may respond with [[Riot|riot]] police; observers have noted increasing militarization of protest policing. Protests may draw counter-protests, and the two sides can sometimes clash violently. A study of the U.S. [[Civil rights movement|civil rights movement]] found that nonviolent activism tended to produce favorable media coverage and shifts in public opinion, while violent protests generated unfavorable coverage.

Song associated with a movement for [[Protest|protest]] and [[Social change|social change]]. Protest songs belong to the broader category of topical songs and may be folk, classical or commercial in genre. Movements with associated songs include abolition, [[Suffrage|women's suffrage]], the labor movement, civil rights and the anti-war movement. Some protest songs are situational, gaining their meaning from context: "Goodnight Irene" acquired protest associations because Lead Belly, a Black convict and social outcast, wrote it, although it is a love song. Others are abstract and express support for peace or universal brotherhood, as in [[Ludwig van Beethoven]]'s "Ode to Joy," a setting of a poem by [[Friedrich Schiller]]. The sociologist R. Serge Denisoff divided protest songs into "magnetic" songs, which build group solidarity, and "rhetorical" songs, which carry a direct political message, such as [[Bob Dylan]]'s "Masters of War."

Any [[Eukaryote|eukaryotic]] organism that is not an animal, land plant or fungus. Protists do not form a natural group but are a paraphyletic group encompassing the entire eukaryote tree of life, from which land plants, animals and fungi evolved. Most are single-celled, although some form multicellular colonies, giant slime molds or seaweeds with differentiated tissues. They were once classified as a kingdom, Protista, or lumped with plants and animals as [[Algae|algae]] and [[Protozoa|protozoa]]. As producers they are responsible for a large portion of global primary production and carbon fixation, while as consumers and decomposers they regulate fungal and bacterial populations. Some are important parasites, causing diseases such as [[Malaria|malaria]] and toxoplasmosis, and free-living forms can cause harmful algal blooms. Protists make up the majority of eukaryotic diversity, and most remain undescribed.

Reconstructed common ancestor of the [[Indo-European languages]]. No direct record survives; it was reconstructed by the comparative method from documented descendants such as [[Sanskrit]] and [[Latin]]. It is hypothesized to have been spoken as a single language from about 4500 BCE to 2500 BCE, though some estimates differ by more than a thousand years. Its reconstructed [[Morphology (linguistics)|morphology]] included inflectional suffixes, ablaut and accent, with complex systems of declension and conjugation. Asterisks mark reconstructed forms, such as *wódr̥*, the ancestor of English *water*. Its regional [[Dialect|dialects]] diverged over many centuries into the known ancient languages and then the modern Indo-European languages.

Postulated prehistoric ethnolinguistic group of [[Eurasia]]. Knowledge of the Proto-Indo-Europeans comes chiefly from linguistic reconstruction, supplemented by [[Archaeology|archaeology]] and archaeogenetics. They likely lived during the Late Neolithic to [[Chalcolithic]] (6400 to 3500 BC), and mainstream scholars place them in the Pontic–Caspian steppe. Some archaeologists would extend this period back to the Neolithic and suggest alternative origins. By the early second millennium BC, descendants spread across Eurasia, reaching [[Anatolia]] (Hittites), the Aegean ([[Mycenaean Greece]]) and southern Siberia (Afanasievo culture). Widely proposed traits include pastoralism with domesticated cattle, [[Horse|horses]] and dogs, [[Cereal|cereal]] cultivation, the solid wheel and a patrilineal kinship system. Martin L. West described them as a linguistic community, a loose network of clans and tribes rather than a nation.

Very young [[Star|star]] still gathering mass from its parent [[Molecular cloud|molecular cloud]]. It is the earliest phase of [[Stellar evolution|stellar evolution]] and, for a low-mass star like the [[Sun]], lasts about 500,000 years. It begins when a molecular cloud fragment collapses under its own gravity to form an opaque core, and it ends when the infalling gas is depleted, leaving a pre-main-sequence star. Protostars are not powered by hydrogen fusion at their centers; their energy comes largely from shocks on their surfaces and on the surrounding disk. Surrounded by interstellar dust, they are not visible at optical wavelengths and radiate mainly in the [[Infrared|infrared]] and millimeter ranges. Infalling gas first builds a low-mass protostar and then a protoplanetary disk, and because of [[Angular momentum|angular momentum]] conservation, an increasing share of gas hits the disk rather than the star.

Polyphyletic group of single-celled [[Eukaryote|eukaryotes]], either free-living or parasitic. They feed on organic matter such as other microorganisms or debris. The term was coined in 1818 by Georg August Goldfuss, who classified these organisms as [[Animal|animals]]; the word means "first animals" because they often show animal-like behaviors such as motility and predation. Originally the group also included multicellular animals such as rotifers, [[Coral|corals]], [[Sponge|sponges]] and [[Jellyfish|jellyfish]]. In 1848 C. T. von Siebold restricted the group to unicellular forms. The grouping was later judged unjustifiable because it fails to meet modern monophyly standards; the term now loosely describes single-celled [[Protist|protists]] that feed by heterotrophy. Textbook examples include *Amoeba*, *Paramecium*, *Euglena* and *Trypanosoma*.

Geographical and cultural region and historical province of southeastern [[France]]. Stretching from the left bank of the lower Rhône to the Italian border, it is bordered by the [[Mediterranean Sea]] to the south. It largely corresponds to the modern administrative region of Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur, and its largest city and capital is [[Marseille]]. The Romans made it their first province beyond the [[Alps]], calling it *Provincia Romana*, a name that evolved into the present one. Until 1481 it was ruled by the counts of Provence from Aquae Sextiae (today Aix-en-Provence), after which it became a province of the kings of France. It hosted the Avignon papacy in the [[Middle Ages]] and retains a distinct cultural and linguistic identity, particularly in its interior. The Cosquer Cave near Marseille contains drawings of bison, seals, auks, horses and human hands dating to between 27,000 and 19,000 BC.

Simple, traditional saying that expresses a perceived truth based on [[Common sense|common sense]] or experience. Proverbs are often metaphorical and formulaic, and collectively form a genre of [[Folklore|folklore]]. A proverb is a fixed expression, unlike a proverbial phrase, which can be altered to fit a sentence's grammar. In the West, the Bible and medieval Latin, aided by the work of [[Erasmus]], played a considerable role in distributing proverbs. One scholar found "between three hundred and five hundred proverbs that stem from the Bible" in cultures where the Bible is the major spiritual book, while another found that 11 of the 106 most common proverbs across Europe are from the Bible. Defining the genre has proved difficult, but Wolfgang Mieder describes a proverb as a short, generally known sentence of the folk that contains wisdom in a metaphorical, fixed and memorizable form.

Capital and most populous city of [[Rhode Island]]. Founded in 1636 by Roger Williams, a religious exile from the Massachusetts Bay Colony, and named for "God's merciful Providence," the city developed as a port at the head of Narragansett Bay. It was noted for textile manufacturing and later for machine tools, jewelry and silverware. It is the third-most populous city in [[New England]], with 190,934 residents at the 2020 census, and its metropolitan area has about 1.7 million. It has eight hospitals and eight institutions of higher learning, including [[Brown University]], and its economy has shifted toward service industries.

Nearest star to Earth after the [[Sun]], located 4.25 [[Light-year|light-years]] (1.3 parsecs) away in the southern constellation [[Centaurus]]. Discovered in 1915 by Robert Innes, it is a small [[Red dwarf|red dwarf]] too faint to be seen with the naked eye. It is a member of the [[Alpha Centauri]] system, orbiting the AB pair with a period of about 550,000 years. Its mass is about 12.5% of the Sun's, and it is a flare star whose magnetic activity causes sudden increases in brightness. It is expected to remain on the main sequence for another four trillion years.

[[Exoplanet]] orbiting within the habitable zone of the red dwarf [[Proxima Centauri]]. It orbits about 0.04848 AU (7.253 million km) from its star, with a period of approximately 11.2 Earth days. It is probably a [[Terrestrial planet|terrestrial planet]] with a minimum mass of 1.06 Earth masses and a slightly larger radius than Earth's. Whether it has an atmosphere is unknown, and its star's flares could strip one away. Announced on 24 August 2016 by the European Southern Observatory, it was confirmed through several years of Doppler spectroscopy measurements. It is among the closest known exoplanets to the [[Solar System]].

Intermediary server application between a client and the server that provides a requested resource. The client sends its request to the proxy, which evaluates it and may provide benefits such as load balancing, privacy or security. A forward proxy is an Internet-facing proxy that retrieves data from a wide range of sources. A reverse proxy is an internal-facing proxy in front of one or more servers, commonly performing load balancing, [[Authentication|authentication]], decryption and caching. In 2008 Gordon Lyon estimated that "hundreds of thousands" of open proxies, accessible to any Internet user, operate on the Internet.

[[Germany|German]] state centered on the North European Plain, which existed from 1525 to 1947. It originated from the 1525 secularization of the Prussian part of the State of the [[Teutonic Order]], and the House of Hohenzollern ruled it for centuries. The Kingdom of Prussia was proclaimed in 1701 and [[Berlin]] became its capital. Under [[Frederick the Great]] (1740–1786), it had a major voice in European affairs. At the [[Congress of Vienna]] (1814–15), Prussia acquired rich new territories, including the coal-rich Ruhr. It became the core of the North German Confederation in 1867 and of the [[German Empire]] in 1871. The kingdom ended in 1918 with the German Revolution. Prussia was de facto dissolved in 1932 by an emergency decree transferring power to Franz von Papen, and it was abolished by an Allied declaration in 1947. The Allies deemed it "a bearer of militarism and reaction."

Dark blue synthetic [[Pigment|pigment]], produced by oxidation of ferrous ferrocyanide salts and also called Berlin blue. It is insoluble in water and is prepared as a very fine colloidal dispersion. It was probably first made around 1706 by paint maker Johann Jacob Diesbach in Berlin, and it is the first modern synthetic pigment. It became prominent in 19th-century Japanese woodblock prints and is the traditional blue of technical blueprints. In medicine, oral Prussian blue is an antidote for [[Thallium|thallium]] and radioactive cesium poisoning and is on the [[World Health Organization|World Health Organization's]] List of Essential Medicines.

Rare and endangered [[Horse|wild horse]] native to the [[Steppe|steppes]] of [[Central Asia]], also called the takhi. It is named after explorer Nikolay Przhevalsky. Once extinct in the wild, it has been reintroduced since the 1990s to [[Mongolia|Mongolia's]] Hustai National Park and elsewhere. It is stockily built, with a typical height of 12–14 hands (48–56 inches, 122–142 cm) and an average weight of around 300 kg (660 lb). It has 33 chromosome pairs, compared with 32 in the domestic horse. Its taxonomic position remains debated, with some classifying it as a [[Species|species]] and others as a subspecies of wild horse.

Statements, beliefs or practices that claim to be scientific but are inherently incompatible with the [[Scientific method|scientific method]]. It is often marked by exaggerated or unfalsifiable claims, reliance on [[Bias|confirmation bias]] rather than attempts at refutation, and continued adherence after experimental discrediting. According to the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, examples include creationism, [[Astrology|astrology]], [[Homeopathy|homeopathy]] and ufology. Pseudoscientific anti-vaccine activism and homeopathic remedies can lead people to forgo medical treatments with demonstrable benefits, and pseudoscientific theories about racial and ethnic classifications have led to [[Racism|racism]] and [[Genocide|genocide]]. The term is often considered pejorative, so its practitioners frequently dispute the label. It is not the same as junk science, which is spurious or fraudulent scientific work.

Order of small, scorpion-like [[Arachnid|arachnids]], also called false scorpions or book scorpions. They are generally beneficial to people because they prey on clothes moth larvae, carpet beetle larvae, booklice, [[Ant|ants]], [[Mite|mites]] and small flies, although they are often mistaken for [[Tick|ticks]] or small [[Spider|spiders]]. They usually range from 2 to 8 mm (0.08 to 0.31 in) in length, with the largest known species, *Garypus titanius* of [[Ascension Island]], reaching 12 mm (0.5 in). Their pedipalps end in pincers that resemble a [[Scorpion|scorpion]]'s, but the [[Abdomen|abdomen]] is short and rounded rather than ending in a tail and stinger. They breathe exclusively through tracheae rather than book lungs. They often use phoresis, attaching to larger animals for transport. Females carry fertilized eggs in a brood pouch on the abdomen, and between two and 50 young hatch in a single brood.

Naturally occurring tryptamine [[Alkaloid|alkaloid]] found in more than 200 species of [[Mushroom|mushrooms]], with hallucinogenic and serotonergic effects. The body converts it into psilocin, which acts on [[Serotonin|serotonin]] receptors, especially the 5-HT2A receptor. Its onset is about 20 to 50 minutes when taken orally, and effects last 4 to 6 hours. Albert Hofmann isolated it in 1958 from *Psilocybe mexicana*. It is a Schedule I controlled substance under the 1971 UN Convention on Psychotropic Substances. It is being studied as a treatment for [[Depression (mood)|depression]] and [[Obsessive–compulsive disorder|obsessive–compulsive disorder]]. It was approved for treatment-resistant depression in [[Australia]] in 2023.

Informal, polyphyletic group of hallucinogenic fungi that contain the prodrug [[Psilocybin|psilocybin]]. It refers to no single [[Species|species]] but to fungi across several [[Genus|genera]]; the most potent are members of *Psilocybe*, such as *P. azurescens* and *P. semilanceata*. Psilocybin has also been isolated from about a dozen other genera, such as *Panaeolus*, *Inocybe* and *Pluteus*. The [[Mushroom|mushrooms]] were used ritualistically in pre-Columbian [[Mexico]] and are used as recreational drugs. Legal status varies: some U.S. states have decriminalized them or allowed therapeutic use, while international treaties generally regulate only the active compounds, not the mushrooms themselves.
